tagline: Electric fields create a twist - not a push
audio_script: Here is the surprising part: an electric field can make an object rotate even when the total force is zero. Imagine a tiny dipole, with plus and minus charges separated by a distance. The field pushes the positive charge one way and the negative charge the other way. Those forces cancel as a net force, but because they act at different points, they create a torque. The torque is p E sine theta. So the dipole keeps turning until it lines up with the field. That is the real picture behind the formula: a uniform field does not translate the dipole. It twists it into alignment.

header_title: Why Electric Flux Cares About Enclosed Charge
tagline: The surface tells you what is inside
audio_script: Picture an invisible bubble around a charge. Now ask a very simple question: how much electric field passes through the bubble? That is electric flux. Here is the key idea: field lines can enter and leave the surface, but only charge trapped inside can create a net imbalance. A charge outside sends field through one side and back out another, so its total contribution cancels. A charge inside cannot cancel that way. Gauss's law turns this picture into one line: total electric flux equals enclosed charge divided by epsilon zero. The important word is enclosed. You are not counting every charge in the universe. You are measuring the net source hidden inside your chosen surface.

header_title: A Projectile Is Two Motions at Once
audio_script: Why does a thrown ball make a parabola? Because the ball is secretly doing two simple things at the same time. Sideways, it keeps moving at constant speed. Up and down, gravity changes its velocity every second. Write those motions separately: x equals u cos theta times t, and y equals u sin theta times t minus one half g t squared. Now remove time between them, and the parabola appears. There is no mysterious curved force pulling the ball along the arc. The curve is what you get when constant horizontal motion is combined with uniformly accelerated vertical motion. That is a powerful physics trick: split a complicated motion into independent pieces, then put the pieces back together.

header_title: Why a Magnetic Field Bends Motion
tagline: Magnetic force changes direction - not speed
audio_script: A magnetic field can bend a moving charge without making it move faster. How? The magnetic force points sideways, perpendicular to the velocity. The Lorentz force is q times v cross B for the magnetic part. Because the force is perpendicular to motion, it changes the direction of the velocity, not its magnitude. So a charged particle can curve into a circle. For uniform magnetic field and fixed speed, the radius is m v divided by the absolute value of q times B. Notice what the equation is really saying: stronger magnetic field, tighter circle; heavier particle, wider circle; faster particle, wider circle. The formula becomes obvious once you keep one geometric fact in mind: the force points sideways.

header_title: How a Lens Knows Where to Focus
tagline: Refraction turns many rays into one image
audio_script: A lens looks simple, but why do parallel light rays meet at one point? The answer is refraction. Light changes direction when it crosses between materials, and the curved surfaces make the amount of bending depend on where the ray hits. A well-designed convex lens turns a whole family of incoming parallel rays toward the same focal point. The lens formula then connects object distance, image distance, and focal length. But the deeper idea is not the algebra. A lens is a device that uses geometry and refraction to make many different paths agree at one location. That is why cameras, eyes, and microscopes can form sharp images. The formula is just a compact way of describing that coordination.

header_title: Two Waves Can Cancel Each Other
tagline: Interference is addition you can see
audio_script: Here is one of the strangest things waves can do: two waves can meet and produce almost nothing. The trick is that waves add. Take one wave with a positive displacement and another with the same size but opposite displacement. At that instant, the sum is zero. This is destructive interference. Shift the timing so the crests line up with crests, and the amplitudes reinforce instead. Constructive interference happens when the path difference is an integer number of wavelengths. Destructive interference happens for half-integer wavelengths. So interference is not waves fighting each other. Each wave keeps moving. The total pattern simply comes from adding their displacements point by point. That single idea explains colors in thin films, noise cancellation, and many optical experiments.

tagline: The circuit has a built-in clock
audio_script: Connect a resistor and capacitor to a battery, and the current does not simply stay constant. It fades away. Why? At the beginning, the capacitor has no stored voltage, so the full battery voltage appears across the resistor and the current is large. As charge builds on the capacitor, its voltage rises. That leaves less voltage across the resistor, so the current falls. The result is an exponential curve: charge grows like one minus e to the minus t over R C. The product R C acts like a clock. After one time constant, the capacitor has reached about sixty-three percent of its final charge. So the circuit is not delaying by magic. It is continuously using the capacitor's growing voltage to reduce its own charging current.

header_title: Where Is Electric Field Energy Stored?
tagline: Energy can live in the field itself
audio_script: Where does the energy go when you charge a capacitor? It is tempting to say, inside the plates. But the more useful picture is that the energy is stored in the electric field between them. The energy density is one half epsilon zero E squared. That tells you something profound: stronger field means disproportionately more energy, because the energy scales with E squared. Integrate that density over the volume, and you get the total stored energy. For an ordinary capacitor, the same result becomes one half C V squared. These are not two different ideas. One is the field picture, the other is the circuit shortcut. When physics gives you both, trust the field picture first. It often tells you where the energy really is.

header_title: Potential Is Not the Same as Field
tagline: One is a number - one is a direction
audio_script: Electric potential and electric field sound like the same thing, but they answer different questions. Potential is a scalar: one number assigned to each point. Electric field is a vector: it tells you the direction and strength of the push on a positive test charge. The connection is a spatial slope. The field points in the direction where potential drops most rapidly, captured by E equals minus the gradient of V. Think of a hill. Height is like potential. Slope is like field. You can stand at a particular height without knowing the direction of the steepest descent, but once you know the landscape, the slope tells you how a ball wants to move. This picture makes the minus sign feel natural instead of arbitrary.

tagline: Changing fields keep each other alive
audio_script: What is light made of? A changing electric field creates a changing magnetic field, and the changing magnetic field creates a changing electric field. The two variations travel together through space. That is an electromagnetic wave. In empty space, the wave speed is c equals one over the square root of mu zero epsilon zero. The electric and magnetic fields are perpendicular to each other, and both are perpendicular to the direction of travel. That geometry is the important picture. Light is not a stream that needs a material medium to carry it. The fields themselves are the traveling disturbance. Once you visualize the fields regenerating one another as the wave moves, the existence of electromagnetic radiation becomes much less mysterious.

header_title: One Face of a Cube Gets How Much Flux?
question_text: A point charge q is placed at the center of a cube. The electric flux through one face is what fraction of q divided by epsilon zero?
audio_script: Here is a classic symmetry test. A point charge sits exactly at the center of a cube. How much electric flux passes through one face? Do not start integrating the electric field. First notice the symmetry: all six faces are equivalent. Gauss's law gives the total flux through the entire cube as q divided by epsilon zero. Six identical faces must therefore share that flux equally. So one face gets q divided by 6 epsilon zero. The answer is option B. The lesson is bigger than this one problem: when a problem gives you strong symmetry, use it before calculus. The geometry has already done most of the work for you.

tagline: PYQ - range is a symmetry problem
question_text: For a projectile launched with speed u on level ground, which angle gives maximum horizontal range?
audio_script: Which angle throws a projectile the farthest on level ground? You do not need a table. The range is u squared times sine 2 theta divided by g. So the whole problem collapses to one question: when is sine 2 theta largest? Its maximum value is one. That happens when 2 theta equals 90 degrees, giving theta equals 45 degrees. Notice the physics behind the answer. A low angle gives plenty of horizontal speed but not enough airtime. A high angle gives airtime but sacrifices horizontal speed. At 45 degrees, those competing effects balance perfectly. That is why the maximum range is not a coincidence. It is built into the product of the horizontal and vertical components.

header_title: Can a Magnetic Field Speed You Up?
question_text: A charged particle enters a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to its velocity. What happens to its speed?
audio_script: Can a magnetic field make a charged particle go faster? No. The magnetic force is q v cross B, which points perpendicular to the particle's velocity when the motion is perpendicular to the field. A perpendicular force changes direction, but it does no work. Mathematically, force dotted with velocity is zero, so the rate of change of kinetic energy is zero. The particle can curve dramatically while keeping the same speed. That distinction is easy to miss in a formula-heavy problem: changing velocity does not automatically mean changing speed. Velocity is a vector. A magnetic field rotates that vector. This is why charged particles can travel in circles or helices without gaining kinetic energy from a static magnetic field.

header_title: Why Does Light Bend at a Boundary?
tagline: The speed changes - the frequency does not
audio_script: Why does a light ray bend when it enters glass from air? The cleanest answer is that its speed changes. In a medium, light travels at v equals c over n. But its frequency is set by the source, so the frequency stays the same across the boundary. If speed changes while frequency stays fixed, wavelength must change. Snell's law packages the geometry into n one sine theta one equals n two sine theta two. The ray bends because different parts of the wavefront are delayed differently as the wave enters the new material. So do not memorize 'light bends because the medium is denser.' The deeper statement is better: the propagation speed changes, the frequency stays fixed, and the geometry of the wavefront forces a new direction.

header_title: Why Resonance Can Make Things Shake Hard
tagline: Tiny pushes can add up dramatically
audio_script: How can a small repeated force create a huge motion? Resonance. Imagine pushing a swing. Each push may be tiny, but if you push at the right rhythm, every push arrives just when the motion is ready to accept energy. The oscillations build. The same idea appears in bridges, musical instruments, molecules, and electrical circuits. For an ideal LC circuit, the natural angular frequency is one over the square root of L C. Drive the system near its natural frequency and the response can become very large, with damping determining how sharp the peak is. Resonance is not extra energy appearing from nowhere. The driver is feeding energy into the system with exactly the timing that makes those contributions add instead of cancel.
